title: Yakubboev Continues Freestyle Friday Championship Push
summary:
GM Nodirbek Yakubboev won in a tense final round of Freestyle Friday on November 6 to lock up victory ahead of second-place GM Ian Nepomniachtchi. Both players improved their position in the standings for the Freestyle Friday Championship (FFC), Yakubboev nearly moving into second place and Nepomniachtchi joining the top eight, with only four more tournaments left in the cycle before the Freestyle World Championship field is decided.

5 | GM | Parham Maghsoodloo | 43 | In a qualifying position

8 | GM | Ian Nepomniachtchi | 30 | In a qualifying position

GM Jan Gustafsson commentated for Freestyle Chess, which you can view below:

Neither Yakubboev nor Nepomniachtchi had the fastest start, with Yakubboev drawing and Nepomniachtchi losing in the second round. The only players to begin 4/4 were GMs Hans Niemann and Fabiano Caruana, and both came back from bad situations ("deep, deep trouble" per Gustafsson) in the fourth round to do so. Caruana got White in their fifth-round encounter, but Niemann held sway most of the game, and won a pawn ending Gustafsson called out from a study.

Niemann's run didn't last much longer, with GM Arseniy Nesterov—who had dropped Yakubboev to 3.5/5 in the fifth round—defeating him in the sixth round. The other player who entered the round with 4.5/5, 13-year-old IM Sergey Sklokin-Bagiyan, lost to Nepomniachtchi. Seven players now had 5/6, including Niemann but not Caruana, whom GM Gata Kamsky beat to become another player on five points.

Nepomniachtchi went on to take out Nesterov in the seventh round, with Niemann and Kamsky keeping pace by defeating FM Artin Ashraf and GM Vladimir Fedoseev, respectively. Nepomniachtchi then convincingly kept things going against Niemann to take the sole lead into the last break, as Kamsky lost with Black against Yakubboev. GMs Alexey Sarana and Nils Grandelius joined Yakubboev on 6.5/8. Against Nepomniachtchi, Niemann hadn't even moved a piece on a whole half of the board by move 15, and less than 10 moves later he was lost.

The decisive game of the tournament was soon to come, in the ensuing round. Yakubboev (who scored a perfect 6/6 after the fifth round) got the better of the opening, but Nepomniachtchi was making him earn the full point until a sudden blunder on move 43 confirmed a new leader (then new coleaders, after Grandelius defeated Sarana).

By now Niemann had remained in contention, with Ashraf and GM Oleksandr Bortnyk fighting their way back into it. In the 10th round, however, Yakubboev and Nepomniachtchi really began separating from the pack. Nepomniachtchi recovered quickly from his ninth-round setback, needing 22 moves to knock Grandelius down, while Ashraf ended Bortnyk's streak to stay a half-point back with Nepomniachtchi. Yakubboev retained the lead with his win over Niemann, however, when Niemann tried to run with his king but quickly saw it trapped on the edge of the board, about to be checkmated when he resigned.

Yakubboev had White against Ashraf in the last game the leader needed. Yakubboev had trouble getting things going, though, and while his game was still very much in the balance, Nepomniachtchi defeated IM Khuong Duy Dau. Fortunately for Yakubboev, he later won a piece from a pin and soon claimed his tournament victory. The win was his second in Freestyle Friday, following a victory on April 24.

After Yakubboev on 9.5 points and Nepomniachtchi on nine, no one else had more than eight. Grandelius and Ashraf took the final spots in the top four on tiebreaks, while everyone in the top 10 made progress in the FFC, including Bortnyk (sixth place today), Niemann (seventh), Kamsky (eighth), and Sklokin-Bagiyan (ninth). GM Alexandra Kosteniuk took home the women's prize and 10 points in the women's FFC standings.

title: Nakamura, Maghsoodloo, Movahed Take 3 0 Thursday Titles
summary:
GMs Hikaru Nakamura and Parham Maghsoodloo both continued their recent 3 0 Thursday successes on November 5, winning the first two tournaments. GM Sina Movahed joined them by winning the third tournament, his first victory since March 19. Meanwhile, WFM Veronika Shubenkova took the top women's prize in the first tournament with seven points, her fifth such victory in 3 0 Thursdays. IM Nurgyul Salimova took the women's prize in the second and third tournaments with six and seven points, respectively.

First Tournament: Nakamura Undefeated

Nakamura streamed his way to victory in the first tournament of the day, confidently winning his first eight games. In the sixth round, he scored a convincing attacking victory against GM Ian Nepomniachtchi.

His toughest test came in the eighth round against GM Magnus Carlsen, who had won six in a row after missing the opening round of the tournament. Nakamura won in a queen and rook endgame, later recording an analysis for his fans.

With a lead on the field, Nakamura was able to cruise to victory, drawing two of his remaining three games and winning the event with 10 points. GM Haik Martirosyan took second place with nine points, ahead of IM Matvey Galchenko on tiebreaks.

The top 10 finishers in the first tournament.

Second Tournament: Maghsoodloo Continues Great Form

Maghsoodloo won four 3 0 Thursday Tournaments in October. He continued November right where he left off, taking clear first in the second tournament of the day. He won his first six games, including a messy GOAT Horns Variation battle against GM Nodirbek Yakubboev in the third round.

Now in the clear lead, Maghsoodloo allowed a draw with Nepomniachtchi in the seventh round. That gave him 6.5/7 entering the next game with Black against GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave.

After a draw with GM Jose Martinez in the ninth round, Maghsoodloo faced Nakamura, who was gunning for a second consecutive tournament victory. That game ended in a draw by repetition, allowing Maghsoodloo to maintain the lead. In the final round, he secured victory with a decisive win against IM Reza Mahdavi. That brought Maghsoodloo to 9.5 points, ahead of Vachier-Lagrave and GM Jules Moussard, who had nine points each.

The top 10 finishers in the second tournament.

Third Tournament: Movahed In Clear First

In the third tournament, Movahed won his first three games. The third was a crushing attack against Moussard.

After a fourth round loss to GM Ray Robson, Movahed got back on track with three consecutive wins. The critical game of the tournament was his ninth-round battle with GM Arjun Erigaisi. Last month, Arjun won a complicated King's Indian Defense to take a 3 0 Thursday ahead of Movahed. This time, Movahed got in trouble, but escaped amid a torrent of complications.

That win gave Movahed 7.5/9, and he finished strong to take sole first place with nine points. For the second time in the day, Martirosyan took second place, this time with 8.5 points. Robson claimed third with eight points.

The top 10 finishers in the third tournament.

3 0 Thursday is a set of three weekly Swiss tournaments for verified titled players featuring their favorite time control. Each of the three tournaments is an 11-round Swiss with a 3+0 time control. The combined prize fund is $3,000 every week.

title: Chess Returns To Esports World Cup In 2027 As Carlsen Targets Third Title
summary:
GM Magnus Carlsen will have the chance to make it three titles in three appearances as chess was confirmed for the 2027 Esports World Cup (EWC) today. The event returns to Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, next summer, with qualification already underway through a revamped Champions Chess Tour (CCT).

Carlsen is the only player guaranteed a place as the defending champion, having cashed in for $250,000 and won his second title after a dominant victory against GM Denis Lazavik in Paris this August. The Norwegian also won the inaugural chess event in Riyadh in 2025 after defeating GM Alireza Firouzja in the final.

Patience, precision, and pressure in every move. The battle of minds returns with Chess at EWC27. ♟️ https://t.co/5jcqo52iN5

— Esports World Cup (@EWC_EN) November 6, 2026

For his potential challengers, the main route to Riyadh runs through the Champions Chess Tour, which began on September 1 and concludes on May 25. Twelve EWC places will be awarded through a leaderboard combining results from Titled Tuesday, the Speed Chess Championship, and the Chess.com Open.

Magnus Carlsen won his second EWC title in Paris this August. Photo: Esports World Cup.

The biggest change is the removal of the automatic qualification for top-three finishers in the Speed Chess Championship and Chess.com Open. Those events will contribute points toward the overall standings, with winners earning 150 points.

Organizers have separately announced a satellite qualifying program that includes chess. Winners of approved satellite events will earn entry into an EWC Last Chance Qualifier, where they will compete for main-event places. Details of the participating tournaments and available places are still to come.

In the second edition of EWC, Carlsen, who represents Team Liquid, defeated GMs Nihal Sarin and Firouzja in the knockout stages before beating Lazavik 3-1 in each of the final's two sets.

The 19-year-old Lazavik, playing for All Gamers (AG), provided one of the biggest stories of the 2026 tournament by eliminating GMs Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Hikaru Nakamura to reach the final, earning $190,000.

Denis Lazavik has proven himself as one of the world's top speed chess specialists. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Chess.com.

In the EWC, the results also matter beyond the chess tournament as players earn points for their esports organizations in an overall Club Championship. Lazavik's runner-up finish earned 750 points for AG, which went on to win the $7 million club title. His semifinal victory also denied points to rival Team Falcons, which is Nakamura's team.

Specific dates for the events, a prize fund, and the full format for the 2027 chess event have not yet been announced. For now, Carlsen is watching the online race to join him in Riyadh.

title: World Junior Rapid Championship 2026: Khumoyun Begmuratov and Eline Roebers capture titles
summary: Khumoyun Begmuratov of Uzbekistan and Eline Roebers of the Netherlands triumphed at the FIDE World Junior Rapid Championship 2026, winning the titles in the Open and Girls sections, respectively. His Excellency Dr. Sultan bin Saif Al Neyadi, UAE Minister of State for Youth Affairs, made the ceremonial first move in the ninth and final rapid round before crowning the champions at the Danat Al Ain Resort. The occasion was attended by Hisham Ali Al Taher, Secretary-General of the Asian Chess Federation, Managing Director and CEO of the Al Ain Chess & Mind Games Club, and Tournament Director. He also helped present the trophies and medals alongside His Excellency Counsellor Yousif Al Afreet Al Kuwaiti, Board Member and Treasurer of the club. Bringing together 185 players from 40 countries competing for four world titles, the championship showcases the next generation of international chess talent and reinforces Al Ain’s standing as a host of major global chess events. Held from November 1 to 7 under the patronage of His Highness Sheikh Nahyan bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Chairman of the Zayed for Good Foundation and Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Sports Council, the event was organised by the Al Ain Chess & Mind Games Club in cooperation with the UAE Chess Federation, under the supervision of FIDE. The opening of the decisive round was also attended by José Antonio Carrillo, President of the Confederation of Chess for the Americas; Javier Ochoa, President of the Ibero-American Chess Federation; and Bernard Wanjala, President of the African Chess Confederation, alongside representatives of the participating delegations. The three officials also joined in presenting the special awards at the subsequent ceremony. In the Rapid Open competition, Uzbekistan’s Khumoyun Begmuratov secured the world title with an unbeaten score of 7.5/9, recording six wins and three draws. India’s Pranav V. claimed silver and Azerbaijan’s Raad Samadov took bronze, both finishing with 7/9, their final positions determined by tiebreaks. Final standings – Open In the Rapid Girls section, Eline Roebers of the Netherlands claimed the world title, scoring 7/9. Uzbekistan’s Umida Omonova earned silver, while Marina Kuznetsova, competing under the FIDE flag, secured bronze. Both finished with 6.5/9, with Omonova taking silver on tiebreaks. Final standings – Girls The medal ceremony brought together players, international chess officials, and delegation representatives to celebrate the new world champions and podium finishers following nine rounds of competition. To celebrate Al Ain’s designation as the Arab Capital of Tourism for 2026, special awards were presented to the best-performing Arab male and female players. Egypt’s Abdalrahman Sameh Mohamed received the Best Arab Player award, while the UAE’s Rouda Essa Alserkal was recognised as the Best Arab Female Player. Ghaith Saeed Al Nuaimi also received the Best Male Player award for the Al Ain Chess & Mind Games Club, while Sheikha Abdulla Almeraikhi received the corresponding Best Female Player award.

title: Crown Prince of Selangor opens FIDE World Amateur Chess Championships in Klang, Malaysia
summary: The FIDE World Amateur Chess Championship 2026 commenced in Klang, Malaysia on November 5. The event attracted 392 players competing across three rating sections: Under-2300, Under-2000 and Under-1700. Each section features separate Open and Women’s 9-round Swiss tournaments with classical time control. A number of disabled players from the host nation’s para-multisport contingent also participate.  The championship is organized by Selangor Chess Association under the auspices of the International Chess Federation (FIDE) and the Malaysian Chess Federation. His Highness Tengku Amir Shah ibni Sultan Sharafuddin Idris Shah Alhaj, Crown Prince of Selangor, officially opened the FIDE World Amateur Chess Championships 2026 at the KSL Esplanade Hotel in Klang. The Crown Prince attended as the Royal Patron of the Tournament and played a friendly blitz game against the FIDE Representative, British Grandmaster Nigel Short. The game ended in a draw. Malaysian players upset the top two seeds The host nation made a strong start in the Open Under-2300 championship. On board one, Nik Ahmad Farouqi (1999) won against Hungary’s top-seeded FM Gyula Mester (2277) with the black pieces. On board two, Tin Shan Wen (1998) defeated Colombia’s second-seeded FM Ramon Junior Gonzalez Parejo (2261) with White. Malaysia also secured a point on board six, where CM Shen Ree Herng (1976) prevailed over FM Ammar Sedrani (2223) of the United Arab Emirates. In the Women’s Under-2300 championship, WCM Nithyalakshmi Sivanesan of Malaysia, WCM Kristina Kim of Kazakhstan and WCM Mumtozbegim Mansurova of Uzbekistan each scored a full point in the opening round. WACC-2026 – Full results Sunday, November 8, is a rest day, while the final round and closing ceremony are scheduled for Thursday, November 12. title: Review: The Petroff Defence - Fight for More Than Equality by GM Fabien Libiszewski
summary:
For a long time, the Petroff Defence had a reputation for being a purely drawish opening – reliable but dry. Those days are over, however. In a ChessBase video course, Grandmaster Fabien Libiszewski demonstrates how modern players can turn this old reputation to their psychological advantage. Christian Höthe took a close look at the course. | Photos: ChessBase

It pays to know the Petroff Defence well, as White often has a false sense of security while Black pursues dynamic plans to play for a win. The highlight of Fabien Libiszewski's video course is the highly topical lines featuring an early 6...Bf5 , which break the symmetry, aim for active play and a space advantage, and confront White with unexpected problems.

A look at the repertoire

Over a total running time of five and a half hours, the French grandmaster guides viewers through a complete repertoire that has been tested by elite grandmasters. The course is divided into clearly defined strategic sections:

The absolute main line: The focus here is on the modern approach with 6...Bf5 after 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.d4 d5 6.Bd3 .

Libiszewski carefully analyses all of White's responses, including the sharp 7.O-O Be7 8.c4 , the positional plans involving 8.Re1 9.Nbd2 , and lines with 9.c4 .

Early deviations on moves 4 and 5: The course leaves no gaps. It covers the modern 4.Nd3 , known from Niemann against Nepomniachtchi, as well as the often underestimated 5.Qe2 Qe7 6.d3 Nf6 7.Nc3 , analysed using games between elite players such as Carlsen and Caruana. The tricky 5.Nc3 also receives in-depth analysis (5...Nf6 6.d5 Be7 7.Bd3 O-O 8.h3).

The modern centre with 3.d4 : Black is given tailor-made responses to both 3...Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5 5.Nxe5 and the variation with 4.dxe5 .

Surprise weapons and sidelines: For quick use in rapid chess or online blitz, Libiszewski introduces the cheeky 3...Nxe4!? immediately after 3.Nxe5 . The Three Knights Game (3.Nc3) and all alternatives on moves 2 and 3 are also covered.

The technical implementation makes full use of the ChessBase infrastructure. The content can be accessed across platforms via the app on Windows and Mac, is available as a ChessBase Book or download, and can also be streamed directly through the ChessBase video portal.

The grandmaster actively involves the learner by pausing the video to ask test questions. When the user enters a move on the demonstration board, immediate video feedback follows, praising correct plans and clearly explaining why typical incorrect ideas do not work. The newly acquired knowledge can be put to the test directly against the Fritz engine in a training game using the Fritz Online web application. The Opening web app offers automated playback of variation trees, allowing users to systematically memorise the correct move sequences. The video window impresses with its clear notation display and powerful toolbar. With a click, users can pause the video to enter their own moves or activate any chess engine installed locally on their PC. Features such as the LiveBook and Assisted Analysis provide continuous support.

The package includes a comprehensive database of model games and a repertoire database. All analyses can be integrated directly into the user's own digital opening book. Using the Opening Reference and Game Reference features, users can replay and examine variations on the analysis board and compare them with grandmaster practice. The integrated Replay Training also ensures a thorough understanding of the resulting middlegame structures.

Conclusion

The Petroff Defence – Fight for More Than Equality is a modern training tool. Fabien Libiszewski provides the perfect preparation for tournament players who want to approach 1.e4 with psychological finesse. An unreserved recommendation to buy – both for digital training at home and for practical tournament play!

The product was provided to the author by ChessBase.

About the author:

Fabien Libiszewski, born in 1984 in Saint-Étienne, is a French chess grandmaster, coach and author.

He earned the grandmaster title in 2009. He reached his peak Elo rating of 2547 in 2016. In the same year, he served as captain of the French national team at the Chess Olympiad in Baku.

Libiszewski remains an active player and has regularly published training courses for ChessBase since 2018, particularly on various opening systems. In 2015, he also worked as a chess consultant and appeared as an actor in the feature film “Le Tournoi”.

title: Who will become the FIDE World Combined Champion?
summary:
The Total Chess World Championship series is a new tournament format combining three different time controls: fast classic, rapid and blitz. The winner of the series will be crowned the FIDE World Combined Champion. Both the winner and the runner-up will then qualify for the Candidates Tournament for the classical World Championship. How did this format come about? | Photo: Michal Walusza / Norway Chess

The FIDE World Combined Champion

In sporting competition, the aim is always to find out who is better. And at the next level, of course, people also want to know who is the very best in a particular sport or discipline.

The best of the best

Even before the "invention" of World Championships, there was always one chess player who was regarded as the best. Philidor, Anderssen and Morphy, for example. From Steinitz onwards, there was a certain formalisation of the contests for the World Championship. The world champion was the player who had defeated the previous world champion in a match for the title. After Alekhine's death, FIDE took over responsibility for awarding the title and introduced fixed rules for organising the World Championships. They were well-thought-out rules: Zonal and Interzonal tournaments in the first year, Candidates Tournaments or Candidates matches in the second, and the World Championship match in the third. Some rules, however, were complete nonsense – the right to a rematch, for example.

Before Elo ratings were introduced, it was largely a matter of perception whether the world champion was also the world's best player. Elo ratings provided a second criterion. The succession of world champions Fischer, Karpov, Kasparov, Kramnik, Anand and Carlsen more or less represented the best players in the world in their respective eras.

There can be only one

The dispute between FIDE president Campomanes and Kasparov led Kasparov and Short to play their 1993 World Championship match outside FIDE. For many years afterwards, there were two chess world champions, which was not good for the standing of chess in the sporting world or elsewhere. Campomanes' successor also dismantled the old World Championship format by introducing annual knockout World Championships, which likewise damaged the prestige of the world title.

In 2006, the two World Championships were finally reunified. The match between Kramnik and Topalov, however, went down in history as a particularly scandal-ridden affair. After years of criticism, FIDE finally abandoned the knockout format for the World Championship and returned to a match format in 2008.

Instead of the former three-year cycle, however, FIDE now introduced a two-year cycle and also changed the qualification paths for finding a challenger several times.

Too many World Championship matches

With the two-year cycle, the world champion now had to defend the title every two years rather than every three years as before. The patient Anand dutifully went along with this, but his successor Carlsen lost his enthusiasm for the exercise after four title defences in seven years and stepped away in 2023. It is not as if Carlsen no longer enjoys chess - quite the opposite. With well over 8,000 games across all kinds of disciplines, the 16 th world champion is among the players with the most games in the Mega Database and, by a wide margin, the world champion with the most recorded games. By comparison, only 1,024 games by Fischer are known. The vast majority of Carlsen's games, however, were played online at short and very short time controls.

Carlsen's departure as world champion created a legitimacy problem for FIDE's flagship World Chess Championship. Carlsen continued playing in all kinds of formats, won one online tournament after another and collected titles at the World Rapid and Blitz Championships. He also continued to lead the world rankings by a substantial margin.

The less imposing successors

For Carlsen's successors on the World Championship throne, however, the world champion's mantle proved far too large. The 17 th world champion, Ding Liren, struggled with mental health problems after winning the title and fell sharply in the Elo rankings. It was similar with the 18 th world champion, Gukesh Dommaraju. Kramnik had already faced criticism after winning his title because he was only second or third in the world rankings. Now the chess world champions were ranked somewhere among the also-rans.

In his talks with FIDE, Carlsen had already proposed other formats. The Norwegian was frustrated by matches lasting several weeks, the endless preparation and the possibility – or necessity – of preparing openings with extreme precision using engines. In his view, the actual playing of chess, where the better player could demonstrate his strengths, was being lost. Carlsen put forward alternative formats, and FIDE has now accepted the idea of a format combining different time controls, apparently not coincidentally proposed by the Norway Chess organisers, featuring the disciplines of Fast Classic, Rapid and Blitz.

New formats wanted

The format is not entirely new, of course, as a tournament of this kind has been played in Biel for several years. The Swiss call it a "triathlon", which describes it quite well. Under FIDE, the format is called "Total Chess". Presumably the Norwegians came up with that name too. The whole thing is the "Total Chess World Championship Tour".

FIDE has not always had the happiest touch when it comes to naming things. "Grand Swiss" is another example – the "big Swiss", or what exactly? Who outside the chess world is supposed to understand that? Is the Total Chess World Championship now somehow more than the World Championship? And is the Total Chess world title worth more than the world title?

Of course, the Total Chess World Championship Tour is not supposed to have a higher status than the (absolute? classical? normal?) World Championship. FIDE is nevertheless giving the format considerable importance by making the Total Chess World Championship Tour a qualification path for the Candidates Tournament. The two best players in the Total Chess series will be able to play in the next Candidates Tournament.

Candidates regulations...

In Total Chess, the three disciplines are Fast Classic (45 minutes + 30 seconds), Rapid (15+10) and Blitz (3+2). A match consists of one Fast Classic game, two Rapid games and four Blitz games. Naturally, the scoring is weighted differently, with eight points for the Fast Classic game, four points for a Rapid game and two points for a Blitz game. Please memorise that before next time.

The whole competition is conceived as a series of three tournaments in different locations. Twenty-four players take part in the events. Tour points are awarded according to finishing position. The top four in the overall standings then meet in the Grand Final.

Explainer video

Total or combined world champion?

The winner of the Grand Final at the end is not, in fact, the Total Chess World Champion, but the FIDE World Combined Champion. There may have been discussions behind the scenes about what to call the title, but having two names (Total Chess and Combined Chess) for the same thing is not really ideal either.

Next Tuesday, things get under way in Budapest with a pilot event. The event begins with the opening ceremony and a Blitz tournament, as is familiar from Norway Chess events. The result of the Blitz tournament will later serve as a tiebreak in the event of players finishing level on points. A group stage with four groups of six players then follows. The four group winners advance to the knockout stage, with semifinals and a final.

Not all, but many of the current top players will be competing in Budapest, along with several other strong players. Magnus Carlsen is among them, and from a German perspective, it is particularly pleasing that Vincent Keymer is also taking part.

The Total Chess organisers have also already created a combined world ranking based on FIDE's Classical, Rapid and Blitz ratings. Magnus Carlsen's lead over the rest is even larger there than usual.

The Total Chess world ranking...

And this is how it works...

An interesting question: if Magnus Carlsen wins the Total Chess World Championship Tour, will he then also play in the Candidates Tournament for the classical World Championship? Or will he be content with the title of FIDE World Combined Champion?

title: Loek van Wely: 10 Chess Principles That Actually Matter
summary:
In his new course, GM Loek van Wely shares ten practical principles from a career spanning 14 Olympiads, eight Dutch championship titles and decades of games against Karpov, Kasparov, Anand and Carlsen. Instead of opening lines, he focuses on how decisions are really made at the board: managing your clock around the critical moments, knowing when to simplify, staying objective about mistakes and recognising the right moment to take a risk. He also covers the psychological side of chess, from not being intimidated by stronger opponents to trusting your own calculation under pressure. A course about the part of chess that opening theory can’t teach you.

10 Chess Principles That Actually Matter

by Loek van Wely

Opening theory gets all the attention. But according to GM Loek van Wely, a player who has played in 14 Olympiads, is eight-time Dutch champion, and has decades of experience against Karpov, Kasparov, Anand, and Carlsen, most of what separates strong players from the rest has nothing to do with memorised lines.

Free sample video: Introduction

Free sample video: Don't Bluff the Donkey

In this course, Van Wely breaks down ten practical principles he's used throughout his career, and that he still sees even grandmasters get wrong. Among them: managing your clock around the real turning points of a game rather than reacting too late, knowing when to simplify instead of complicate, staying objective about your own mistakes as well as your opponent's, and recognising the one moment to take risks before it's too late to matter. He also addresses the psychological side of the game: not being intimidated by a strong opponent's body language or time pressure, and trusting your own calculations even against higher-rated players.

This isn't a course on lines or theory. It's a look at how decisions actually get made (and also mishandled) at the highest level, and how to apply that awareness to your own games.

What you'll get:

• Ten practical principles drawn directly from a top grandmaster's tournament career

• Guidance on time management, risk-taking, and staying objective under pressure

• Real examples and stories from decades of play against World Champions

• Insight into the psychological side of chess that opening books never cover

The part of chess that opening theory can't teach you.

title: Bavarian Championship: Gopal emerges as sole leader
summary:
Indian grandmaster G.N. Gopal has taken the sole lead at the Bavarian Chess Championship in Gmund am Tegernsee, reaching 5½/6 points after defeating 15-year-old German IM Hussain Besou on Thursday. Twelve players follow half a point behind, including top seed Frederik Svane, who defeated Polish IM Klaudia Kulon. | Photo: Finn Engesser

Gopal hands Besou his first defeat

Indian grandmaster G.N. Gopal has taken the sole lead at the 29 th Open International Bavarian Chess Championship in Gmund am Tegernsee. The nine-round Swiss tournament, which runs from 31 October to 8 November. Following a fifth round that left six players tied for first place on 4½/5 points, Thursday's sixth round saw Gopal move ahead of the field with 5½ points. Twelve players are now half a point behind the leader.

Gopal secured his fifth victory of the tournament by defeating 15-year-old German IM Hussain Besou, who had joined the leading group the previous day with a win over former world junior champion Peter Acs.

Playing with the black pieces, Besou struggled to find sufficient space for his pieces and gradually came under pressure on the kingside. His defeat ended a run of 15 tournament games without a loss and considerably reduced his chances of obtaining a GM norm in this event. Gopal, meanwhile, has only conceded one draw so far, against fellow Indian GM Krishnan Sasikiran in round five.

The 37-year-old leader, who hails from Kerala in southern India, became his state's first GM in 2007, aged 18. He is no stranger to the tournament at Tegernsee, having finished fourth in the 2023 edition with 7/9 points. His performance rating after six rounds stands at 2734.

G.N. Gopal facing Husain Besou | Photo: Sandra Schmidt

Most of the other encounters between the leading players ended peacefully. Kacper Piorun and Rithvik R Raja agreed to a draw after just 13 moves, while Sasikiran and Emre Can also split the point following a symmetrical game. Nijat Abasov and Sohum Lohia repeated moves to draw after 19 moves, leaving all six players on 5/6 points.

Top seed Frederik Svane, meanwhile, collected a full point against Polish IM Klaudia Kulon, the highest-rated woman in the field. Playing white, Svane obtained a slightly favourable position from a Colle-Zukertort setup before his opponent weakened her kingside on moves 18 and 19. The German GM took advantage of the resulting vulnerabilities to secure his fifth point.

Third seed Alexander Donchenko was less successful against IM Gerlef Meins, who defended an approximately equal rook endgame to hold a draw. Donchenko thus remains on 4½/6.

In the women's standings, Kulon's defeat allowed several competitors to catch up with her on 4/6 points, including Svenja Butenandt and Kateryna Dolzhykova.

Kacper Piorun from Poland and Raja Rithvik R from India signed a quick draw on the top board | Photo: Sandra Schmidt
